lead: However many sources and resistors a linear network holds, at any two of its terminals it behaves exactly like one voltage source in series with one resistor. Thevenin's theorem names them Vth and Rth. Norton's theorem describes the same terminals as one current source IN in parallel with RN = Rth. Once a network is reduced to two numbers, the current in any load follows from one line, which is why engineers model a car battery, a sensor bridge, a mains supply or an amplifier output this way.
prereq: You need: linearity and superposition, nodal or mesh analysis, and source transformation (circuit elements and laws).

blocks.text: Statement. Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced, at its terminals a-b, by a voltage source Vth in series with a resistance Rth. Vth is the open-circuit voltage Voc at a-b. Rth is the resistance seen at a-b with every independent source switched off (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened) and every dependent source left in place.

items: Decide which element is the load and remove it. Everything else stays: the network is all that remains.
Find V<sub>oc</sub> = V<sub>th</sub> across the open terminals, by any method, and mark its polarity (a positive with respect to b).
Switch off the independent sources and find R<sub>th</sub> looking into a-b. With no dependent sources, series-parallel reduction is enough.
Draw V<sub>th</sub> in series with R<sub>th</sub>, put the load back, and find the load current I<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>).

blocks.text: Why it works. Replace the load by a current source of value I. By superposition the terminal voltage is the part due to the internal sources, which is Voc (the I run is switched off), plus the part due to I alone, which is −RthI. So V = Voc − RthI for every load: a straight line, and two numbers fix a straight line. A real network is linear only while its elements are; a battery's internal resistance changes with charge and temperature, so its Thevenin values hold for one condition.
Statement. The same network can be replaced by a current source IN in parallel with RN. IN is the short-circuit current Isc that flows from a to b through a wire joining them, and RN = Rth.
V<sub>th</sub> in volts, I<sub>N</sub> = I<sub>sc</sub> in amperes, R<sub>th</sub> = R<sub>N</sub> in ohms. Any two of V<sub>oc</sub>, I<sub>sc</sub> and R<sub>th</sub> give the third.

This is source transformation applied to the whole network: a voltage source in series with R becomes a current source V/R in parallel with the same R. Choose whichever form makes the next step short: Thevenin for series loads, Norton when loads are added in parallel. Fix the direction of I<sub>N</sub> as the current leaving terminal a through the external short; then both forms push current the same way through a load.
A dependent source cannot be switched off and cannot be merged into a resistance, so series-parallel reduction fails. Use one of two methods.

items: Open circuit and short circuit: find Voc and Isc with all sources on, then Rth = Voc/Isc. Works when the network has at least one independent source.

Test source: switch off the independent sources, keep the dependent ones, apply a test voltage Vt at a-b (or a test current), solve for the current It entering terminal a, and take Rth = Vt/It. Needed when the network has only dependent sources, where Vth = 0 and Isc = 0.

blocks.text: With dependent sources R<sub>th</sub> can come out smaller than any single resistor, or even negative, which means the network can deliver power from its controlled source. That is a real result, not an arithmetic slip; a negative value from a network of resistors and independent sources only, however, is a slip.

examples.question: A 32 V source is in series with 4 Ω. A 12 Ω resistor is connected across the source side, and a 1 Ω resistor runs from the top of the 12 Ω to terminal a; terminal b is the bottom wire (Figure 2.4.1). Find the Thevenin and Norton equivalents at a-b and the current in loads of 2 Ω, 4 Ω and 8 Ω.
steps: Open circuit: no current flows in the 1 Ω, so V<sub>oc</sub> is the voltage across the 12 Ω: V<sub>th</sub> = 32 × 12/(4 + 12) = 24 V, a positive.
Short the 32 V source and look in from a-b: 1 Ω in series with (4 ∥ 12) = 1 + 4 × 12/16 = 1 + 3 = 4 Ω. So R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω.
Norton: I<sub>N</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>/R<sub>th</sub> = 24/4 = 6 A, R<sub>N</sub> = 4 Ω.

Check I<sub>sc</sub> directly: with a-b shorted the 1 Ω is in parallel with the 12 Ω, 12/13 Ω, so the source sees 4 + 12/13 = 64/13 Ω and supplies 32 × 13/64 = 6.5 A. The 1 Ω branch takes 6.5 × 12/13 = 6 A. Same as I<sub>N</sub>.
Loads: I<sub>L</sub> = 24/(4 + R<sub>L</sub>) gives 24/6 = 4 A for 2 Ω, 24/8 = 3 A for 4 Ω and 24/12 = 2 A for 8 Ω.
examples.answer: V<sub>th</sub> = 24 V, R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω; I<sub>N</sub> = 6 A in parallel with 4 Ω; load currents 4 A, 3 A and 2 A.

examples.question: A 12 V source in series with 6 Ω feeds terminal a; iₓ is the current in the 6 Ω towards a. A 12 Ω resistor joins a to b (the reference), and a current-controlled current source of 0.5iₓ drives current from b into a. Find the Thevenin equivalent at a-b and check R<sub>th</sub> with a test source.
steps: Open circuit, v = voltage of a: KCL at a gives iₓ + 0.5iₓ = v/12 with iₓ = (12 − v)/6. So 1.5(12 − v)/6 = v/12; times 12: 3(12 − v) = v, so v = 9 V. V<sub>th</sub> = 9 V.
Short circuit (a joined to b): v = 0, so iₓ = 12/6 = 2 A, the 12 Ω carries nothing, and I<sub>sc</sub> = iₓ + 0.5iₓ = 3 A.

Test-source check: short the 12 V source, keep the controlled source, apply V<sub>t</sub> at a. Now iₓ = (0 − V<sub>t</sub>)/6 = −V<sub>t</sub>/6. KCL at a: I<sub>t</sub> + iₓ + 0.5iₓ = V<sub>t</sub>/12, so I<sub>t</sub> = V<sub>t</sub>/12 + 1.5V<sub>t</sub>/6 = V<sub>t</sub>/12 + 3V<sub>t</sub>/12 = V<sub>t</sub>/3. R<sub>th</sub> = 3 Ω, as before.
Wrong method for comparison: switching off the controlled source gives 6 ∥ 12 = 4 Ω.
A 6 Ω load would draw 9/(3 + 6) = 1 A.
examples.answer: V<sub>th</sub> = 9 V, I<sub>sc</sub> = 3 A, R<sub>th</sub> = 3 Ω (not 4 Ω); a 6 Ω load draws 1 A.

traps: Switching sources off the wrong way. A voltage source becomes a short and a current source an open; reversing them changes R<sub>th</sub>.
Calling a resistor of the network the load. Only the element you remove is the load; in worked example 1 the 12 Ω and 1 Ω stay inside.
Switching off a dependent source when finding R<sub>th</sub>. In worked example 2 that gives 4 Ω instead of 3 Ω.
Getting the sign of I<sub>N</sub> wrong. Take it as the current leaving a through the short, the same direction in which V<sub>th</sub> (a positive) drives a load.
Using the equivalent to find power lost inside the original network. The equivalent is exact only at the terminals; its R<sub>th</sub> loss is not the network's internal loss.

quiz.a: Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced at its terminals by a voltage source V<sub>th</sub>, the open-circuit voltage, in series with R<sub>th</sub>, the resistance seen at the terminals with independent sources switched off.

quiz.q: Why does a load see a linear network only through two numbers?
quiz.a: By superposition the terminal voltage is V = V<sub>oc</sub> − R<sub>th</sub>I for every load current I. That is a straight line, fixed by its intercept V<sub>oc</sub> and slope −R<sub>th</sub>.

quiz.q: A source has V<sub>th</sub> = 9 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 3 Ω. Find the current in a 6 Ω load and the terminal voltage.

A network has only these parts: a 3 Ω resistor from a to node c, and a voltage-controlled voltage source from c (+) to b of value 2Vₓ, where Vₓ = V<sub>a</sub> − V<sub>c</sub> is the voltage across the 3 Ω. Find R<sub>th</sub> at a-b.
quiz.a: No independent source, so V<sub>th</sub> = 0 and a test source is needed. Apply V<sub>t</sub> at a with b at 0 V: V<sub>c</sub> = 2(V<sub>t</sub> − V<sub>c</sub>), so V<sub>c</sub> = 2V<sub>t</sub>/3 and Vₓ = V<sub>t</sub>/3. I<sub>t</sub> = Vₓ/3 = V<sub>t</sub>/9, so R<sub>th</sub> = 9 Ω.

quiz.q: Two different networks have the same V<sub>th</sub> and R<sub>th</sub>. Can any load tell them apart? Where do they differ?
quiz.a: No load connected at a-b can tell them apart: same current, voltage and power for every load. They differ inside, for example in the power their own resistors waste and the current drawn from their sources.

beyond: Datasheets use Thevenin's idea everywhere: a regulator's output impedance, an amplifier's output resistance and a battery's internal resistance are all R<sub>th</sub> at one pair of terminals. Battery-management chips estimate a cell's state of charge from its open-circuit voltage and internal resistance. With more than one pair of terminals the two numbers become a matrix, the two-port parameters. Search for 'output impedance', 'battery equivalent circuit model' and 'two-port parameters'.
